checkpoints: Understand why monorepos improve cross-layer consistency
Initialize a Turborepo workspace with apps/frontend and apps/backend
Share a TypeScript types package between frontend and backend
Run both apps concurrently with a single turbo dev command

content.value: In production teams, keeping frontend and backend in sync is an operational challenge. A monorepo houses both in a single version-controlled repository, enabling shared type definitions and coordinated deployments. Turborepo adds a build orchestration layer: it caches build artifacts and runs tasks in parallel. Create a packages/shared directory with TypeScript interfaces for your API response shapes — import the same interface in both the Flask OpenAPI schema and the React component. Turborepo's pipeline configuration defines the dependency order: frontend's dev task depends on backend's dev task starting first.

moduleTitle: GraphQL API with Strawberry and React
checkpoints: Understand REST vs GraphQL trade-offs
Define a GraphQL schema with Strawberry in Flask
Write queries and mutations from the GraphiQL explorer
Connect React to the GraphQL endpoint with Apollo Client
Implement a subscription for real-time updates

content.value: REST requires multiple round-trips and often over- or under-fetches data. GraphQL lets the client specify exactly what it needs in a single request. Strawberry is a Python GraphQL library with a type-safe, decorator-based API that integrates naturally with Flask. Define types with @strawberry.type, define a Query class with resolver functions, and mount the GraphQL endpoint with GraphQLView. Apollo Client on the React side handles caching, loading state, and polling. Subscriptions add WebSocket-based real-time updates — a GraphQL alternative to Socket.IO.

checkpoints: Install Playwright and configure it to target your running stack
Write a test that registers a user and logs in
Write a test that creates, edits, and deletes a resource
Run tests in CI with GitHub Actions against a test database
Add visual regression tests for key UI components

content.value: Unit and integration tests verify individual layers; end-to-end tests verify the whole system works together. Playwright automates a real browser — it clicks buttons, fills forms, and asserts on DOM state just like a user would. The critical full stack test: register → log in → create a resource → verify it persists → log out → verify it's gone after logout. Run E2E tests in CI against a fresh test database (configured with a test-specific .env) so they never pollute production data. Playwright's trace viewer makes debugging failed CI tests practical.

checkpoints: Write a GitHub Actions workflow that runs backend tests
Add a step that runs frontend tests
Add a deploy step that pushes to Render and Vercel on main
Protect the main branch: require passing CI before merge
Add a status badge to your README

content.value: CI/CD automates the path from code to production. A GitHub Actions workflow triggers on push to main: run backend pytest, run frontend Vitest, and if both pass, trigger deployments. Render and Vercel both offer webhook-based deploys — the workflow calls the deploy hook URL as a final step. Store secrets (API keys, deploy hook URLs) in GitHub Actions secrets, not in the workflow file. Branch protection rules enforce this gate: no direct pushes to main, CI must pass, at least one approval. This turns your side project into a professional, gated release process.

checkpoints: Add structured JSON logging to Flask with python-json-logger
Instrument the React app with Sentry for frontend error tracking
Instrument Flask with Sentry for backend error tracking
Set up a Sentry alert for new high-frequency errors
Trace a user-triggered error from the React console to the Flask log

content.value: You can't fix what you can't see. Structured logging outputs JSON instead of plain text — log lines can be parsed by log aggregators like Datadog or AWS CloudWatch. Use python-json-logger to configure Flask's logger to emit JSON. Sentry captures unhandled exceptions in both layers and links them via a trace ID: one error in React generates a Sentry event that includes the API response, while the corresponding Flask exception appears as a linked server error. Set up an alert for any error that occurs more than five times in an hour — this is your production smoke detector.

checkpoints: Implement a simple flag service in Flask using a database table
Fetch flag values in React at app startup
Gate a UI feature behind a flag check
Toggle the flag in the database and observe the change without a deploy
Design a simple A/B test: 50/50 flag assignment per user

content.value: Feature flags decouple deployment from release — you ship code dark and enable it for users when ready. Build a simple flag service: a Flask endpoint returns { 'new_dashboard': true, 'beta_editor': false } based on flag records in the database. React fetches flags at startup and stores them in a Zustand store. Gate features: if (flags.new_dashboard) return <NewDashboard />. Flipping a flag in the database changes behavior for all users within seconds, with no redeploy. A/B testing extends this: assign users to a variant deterministically (hash the user ID) and log which variant they saw alongside conversion events.

content.value: Your capstone is a production-grade SaaS starter kit — the kind of foundation a startup would build on. It demonstrates advanced full stack skills: monorepo tooling, GraphQL, comprehensive testing, automated deployment, observability, and feature flags. The architecture document in the README is as important as the code: explain why you chose each tool, what trade-offs you made, and what you'd change with more time. This project is not a portfolio piece — it's a platform you could realistically ship a product on.
